_note: HOUSE scenario library for step 5 of the risk tool. The wording is owned by Sam Maesschalck (SolutionsPT, named 14 Nov 2026), who approves any change to it. Every scenario is written in SolutionsPT's own words for this tool and is not taken from any standard, threat framework or vendor document. The SR ids are references to IEC 62443-3-3 system requirements by id only; no requirement text is reproduced. The library holds no ratings: the consultant rates every scenario added from it. Nothing in this note is shown in the tool or printed in a deliverable.

scenarios.title: Vendor remote session misused
scenarios.statement: An external attacker uses stolen or reused credentials for the vendor's remote access path to open a session into the control network and change control logic or set points.
scenarios.source: External attacker using a third party's access
scenarios.entryPoint: Vendor remote access gateway or VPN
scenarios.consequence: Unsafe or unplanned process changes, loss of control, unplanned shutdown
vulnerabilities: Shared or long-lived vendor accounts
No multi-factor authentication on remote access
Sessions not approved or supervised by site staff

countermeasures.description: Require multi-factor authentication for every remote session
Broker vendor sessions through a jump host in the DMZ, approved per session
Record remote sessions and review them

scenarios.title: Ransomware spreads from the business network
scenarios.statement: Ransomware that has entered the business network crosses into the control network through an open or poorly filtered connection and encrypts operator and server hosts.
scenarios.source: Criminal group running ransomware
scenarios.entryPoint: Connection between the business network and the control network
scenarios.consequence: Loss of view and control from the HMIs, and an extended outage while hosts are rebuilt
vulnerabilities: Permissive firewall rules between the business and control networks
One Windows domain shared by business and control hosts
Unpatched operating systems on operator hosts

countermeasures.description: Separate the business and control networks with a DMZ and deny-by-default rules
Malware protection on Windows hosts in the control network
Tested offline backups of control system hosts and configurations

scenarios.title: Infected removable drive on a control host
scenarios.statement: A removable drive carrying malware is plugged into an engineering workstation or HMI, and the malware runs and spreads within the zone.
scenarios.source: Employee or contractor without malicious intent, carrying malware
scenarios.entryPoint: USB port on an engineering workstation or HMI
scenarios.consequence: Compromised hosts in the zone, possible changes to control logic, loss of availability
vulnerabilities: USB ports open on control system hosts
No scanning station for incoming media
User rights that let unknown files run

countermeasures.description: Control removable media with a scanning kiosk and a list of approved devices
Disable unused ports and services on control system hosts
Application allow-listing on engineering workstations

scenarios.title: Engineering workstation used to change controller logic
scenarios.statement: An attacker who has taken over an engineering workstation uses its configuration software to download modified logic to a PLC.
scenarios.source: External attacker with a foothold on the engineering workstation
scenarios.entryPoint: Engineering workstation and its configuration software
scenarios.consequence: The process runs outside its design limits, or faults are hidden until they appear later
vulnerabilities: Configuration software open to any logged-on user
No password or key switch protecting controller changes
No comparison of running logic with a known good copy

countermeasures.description: Named accounts and role-based access to engineering software
Protect controllers against changes outside a maintenance window, by key switch or password
Compare controller logic with the approved version on a schedule

scenarios.title: Safety function altered or bypassed
scenarios.statement: An attacker or a careless change disables or alters a safety instrumented function, so it no longer trips the process when it should.
scenarios.source: Capable attacker targeting safety systems, or unsafe maintenance practice
scenarios.entryPoint: Safety engineering station, or a network shared with the basic control system
scenarios.consequence: Loss of a layer of protection; injury, loss of life or a major release if a demand occurs
vulnerabilities: Safety and basic control share a network or an engineering station
Safety controller left in a mode that accepts changes
Bypasses and overrides not tracked

countermeasures.description: Keep the safety system in its own zone with tightly limited conduits
Physical key or hardware lock for changes to safety logic
Alarm and log any change of mode, bypass or download on the safety controller

scenarios.title: Forged commands on an unauthenticated industrial protocol
scenarios.statement: A device on the control network sends forged or altered commands over an industrial protocol that accepts any sender, changing outputs or set points.
scenarios.source: Attacker with a foothold in the control network
scenarios.entryPoint: Control network carrying unauthenticated protocol traffic, such as Modbus TCP
scenarios.consequence: Unexpected valve or drive movement, process upset, equipment damage
vulnerabilities: Protocol with no authentication or integrity checks
Any host on the segment can reach controller ports
No monitoring for unexpected write commands

countermeasures.description: Limit which hosts can reach controller ports by filtering at the zone boundary
Use protocol variants with message authentication where the devices support them
Monitor control traffic for unexpected write commands

scenarios.title: Plant wireless network reached from outside
scenarios.statement: An attacker within radio range joins a plant wireless network that has weak security and reaches control devices behind it.
scenarios.source: Opportunistic or targeted attacker near the site
scenarios.entryPoint: Plant wireless access point or wireless instrument gateway
scenarios.consequence: Unauthorised access to control devices; false or lost readings
vulnerabilities: Weak or shared wireless keys
Wireless network bridged straight into the control network
Signal reaches beyond the site fence

countermeasures.description: Strong authentication for every wireless client
Put wireless devices in their own zone behind a firewall
Restrict what wireless users can do once connected

scenarios.title: Historian used as a route in
scenarios.statement: An attacker compromises a historian or data server that both business users and the control network can reach, and uses it as a route into the control zone.
scenarios.source: External attacker already present in the business network
scenarios.entryPoint: Historian or replication server reachable from both networks
scenarios.consequence: A foothold inside the control zone; altered or lost production data
vulnerabilities: Dual-homed server spanning both networks
Inbound connections allowed from business users into the control zone
Unpatched database or web service

countermeasures.description: Place a replica historian in the DMZ and send data out one way
Allow only outbound connections from the control zone
Harden and patch servers in the DMZ

scenarios.title: Control network overloaded
scenarios.statement: A flood of traffic, a misbehaving device or a careless scan overloads switches or controllers so that control and visibility are lost.
scenarios.source: Attacker, faulty device or careless network scan
scenarios.entryPoint: Any connected host or switch port in the control network
scenarios.consequence: Loss of view, controllers dropping communication, process trip
vulnerabilities: Controllers with little tolerance for unexpected traffic
No limits on broadcast or traffic rates
Active scanning tools used on the live network

countermeasures.description: Rate limiting and storm control on control network switches
Segment the network so that a fault stays within one zone
Agree rules for scanning and testing on live systems

scenarios.title: Default or shared passwords
scenarios.statement: An attacker or an unauthorised user logs on to an HMI, switch or controller with a default or widely shared password.
scenarios.source: Insider, or an attacker with network access
scenarios.entryPoint: Device web page, console or remote management service
scenarios.consequence: Unauthorised configuration changes, with no record of who made them
vulnerabilities: Factory default passwords never changed
Generic accounts shared by a whole shift
No lockout after failed attempts

countermeasures.description: Change default credentials and give people named accounts
Enforce password strength and lockout
Log logons and configuration changes

scenarios.title: Tampered software update
scenarios.statement: A software update, firmware image or engineering package from a supplier has been tampered with and is installed on control system hosts or devices.
scenarios.source: Attacker in the supplier's build or delivery chain
scenarios.entryPoint: Supplier update, download portal or delivered media
scenarios.consequence: Hidden malicious code on many hosts or devices at once
vulnerabilities: Updates installed without checking signatures or hashes
Updates downloaded straight from the internet onto control hosts
No test system to try updates on first

countermeasures.description: Check signatures or hashes before any update is installed
Stage and test updates on a system that is not in production, and check the security functions still work afterwards
Keep an inventory of installed software and firmware versions

scenarios.title: Insider with engineering rights
scenarios.statement: A disgruntled employee or contractor with legitimate engineering rights deliberately changes the configuration to disrupt production.
scenarios.source: Malicious insider
scenarios.entryPoint: Authorised engineering access
scenarios.consequence: Lost production, damaged equipment, risk to safety
vulnerabilities: Broad standing rights beyond what the task needs
Access not removed promptly when people leave
Changes not reviewed by a second person

countermeasures.description: Least privilege, with access rights reviewed regularly
Remove access promptly when people leave or change roles
Record engineering changes and have them reviewed

scenarios.title: Phished credentials used on OT remote access
scenarios.statement: A phishing email gives an attacker an engineer's credentials, which they then use on the remote access service or jump hosts that serve the control system.
scenarios.source: External attacker
scenarios.entryPoint: Engineer's corporate email, then the remote access portal
scenarios.consequence: The attacker works as a trusted engineer would
vulnerabilities: The same password for corporate and OT accounts
Remote access protected by a password alone
OT accounts held in the corporate directory

countermeasures.description: Separate OT accounts from corporate accounts
Multi-factor authentication for access from untrusted networks
Alert on logons at unusual times or from unusual places

scenarios.title: Control system service exposed to the internet
scenarios.statement: A control system device or remote service is reachable from the internet, and is found and attacked through automated scanning.
scenarios.source: Opportunistic attacker using internet scanning
scenarios.entryPoint: Internet-facing port on a router, modem or cloud connector
scenarios.consequence: Direct remote manipulation of the process
vulnerabilities: Port forwarding left in place after commissioning
Cellular modem fitted by a supplier without the site's knowledge
No regular check of what can be reached from outside

countermeasures.description: Remove direct internet paths and route access through the managed remote access service
Keep an inventory of every external connection, modems included
Check regularly, from outside, what the site exposes

scenarios.title: Values shown to operators falsified
scenarios.statement: An attacker alters the values shown to operators so that the process looks normal while it is driven out of its limits.
scenarios.source: Capable attacker targeting the process
scenarios.entryPoint: Communication between controllers and HMIs
scenarios.consequence: Operators do not act on a real problem; damage or a release follows
vulnerabilities: No integrity protection on traffic between controllers and HMIs
A single source for process values, with no cross check
Network devices that let traffic be intercepted

countermeasures.description: Integrity protection on control communications where supported
Alarm when a critical value disagrees with an independent reading
Detect unexpected devices and address conflicts on the network

scenarios.title: Design or recipe data taken
scenarios.statement: Design drawings, network diagrams, recipes or set points are copied out of the control system and used to plan an attack, or taken by a competitor.
scenarios.source: Industrial espionage, or an attacker preparing a later attack
scenarios.entryPoint: File shares, historians and engineering backups
scenarios.consequence: Loss of intellectual property, and a better informed attacker
vulnerabilities: Documents stored on open shares
Backups and project files not encrypted
No record of who reads design data

countermeasures.description: Restrict and log access to design and recipe data
Encrypt sensitive files when stored and when sent
Wipe data from equipment before it is disposed of

scenarios.title: Backups not there when needed
scenarios.statement: After a failure or an attack the site finds that backups of controller logic and host images are missing, out of date, or encrypted along with everything else.
scenarios.source: Ransomware, hardware failure or poor practice
scenarios.entryPoint: Backup server and backup process
scenarios.consequence: A long outage while systems are rebuilt from scratch
vulnerabilities: Backups kept on the same network as the systems they protect
Restores never tested
Controller logic saved only on one laptop

countermeasures.description: Regular backups held offline or in a separate zone
Test restores to a known state on a schedule
Keep a recovery plan for each critical system

scenarios.title: Contractor laptop connected to the control network
scenarios.statement: A contractor connects their own laptop to the control network for commissioning or fault finding, bringing in malware or opening an uncontrolled path out.
scenarios.source: Contractor without malicious intent, with malware already on the laptop
scenarios.entryPoint: Spare switch port or a network connection in a cabinet
scenarios.consequence: Malware on control hosts, or an unmanaged route to outside networks
vulnerabilities: Open switch ports in cabinets
No check of visiting laptops
Laptop also connected to a mobile network

countermeasures.description: Provide laptops managed by the site for work on the control system
Disable unused switch ports and control which devices can connect
Connect temporary devices only through a dedicated maintenance zone

scenarios.title: Physical access to cabinets and racks
scenarios.statement: Someone gains physical access to a control cabinet, rack room or field junction box and connects a device or changes settings by hand.
scenarios.source: Intruder, visitor or unauthorised staff
scenarios.entryPoint: Unlocked cabinet, rack room or remote outstation
scenarios.consequence: Direct changes to equipment, and a hidden foothold
vulnerabilities: Cabinets and rack rooms left unlocked
No record of who went in
Exposed network ports and console connections

countermeasures.description: Lock cabinets and rack rooms, and keep controller key switches in run
Disable unused ports on devices
Alarm on cabinet doors or device state changes where possible

scenarios.title: Known flaw on an unpatched host
scenarios.statement: An attacker on the network exploits a known flaw in an unpatched operating system or application on an HMI or server.
scenarios.source: Attacker or self-spreading malware already inside the network
scenarios.entryPoint: Network services on control system hosts
scenarios.consequence: The host is taken over, with loss of view or control from it
vulnerabilities: Operating systems past their supplier's support
Patches not approved or applied for long periods
Network services running that are not needed

countermeasures.description: Patch management agreed with the system supplier, based on an inventory of installed versions
Remove or disable services that are not needed
Malware protection where patching is not possible

scenarios.title: Cloud monitoring link used to reach back in
scenarios.statement: A connection that sends plant data to a supplier's or the owner's cloud service is misused to reach back into the control system.
scenarios.source: Attacker who has compromised the cloud service or its credentials
scenarios.entryPoint: Outbound cloud connector or edge gateway
scenarios.consequence: Remote access to the process through a path meant to run one way
vulnerabilities: Connector that also accepts inbound commands
Long-lived keys stored on the gateway
Gateway placed inside the control zone

countermeasures.description: Put the gateway in its own zone and allow traffic one way only
Authenticate the gateway with keys that can be changed
Encrypt data leaving the site

scenarios.title: Attacker works unseen in the control zone
scenarios.statement: An attacker stays in the control zone for weeks, preparing a disruptive attack, because events on hosts and devices are not recorded or reviewed.
scenarios.source: Capable attacker already inside the network
scenarios.entryPoint: Any route into the zone
scenarios.consequence: Late detection, a longer outage and no basis for recovery decisions
vulnerabilities: Logging switched off or overwritten quickly
Clocks not synchronised
Nobody reviews alerts from security tools

countermeasures.description: Collect logs centrally, with enough storage
Synchronise time across the control system
Monitor security events and respond to them

scenarios.title: Firewall and switch settings drift
scenarios.statement: An attacker in the business network reaches the control zone through a firewall rule added for convenience and never removed.
scenarios.source: External attacker, helped by changes made for convenience
scenarios.entryPoint: Firewall and switch management interfaces
scenarios.consequence: Zones that are separate on paper but not in practice, so any attack spreads further
vulnerabilities: Temporary rules never removed
Management interfaces open to the whole network
No baseline of approved settings

countermeasures.description: Keep an approved baseline of network and security settings and compare against it
Review firewall rules on a schedule
Restrict management access to a dedicated network

scenarios.title: Destructive malware aimed at the site
scenarios.statement: A targeted attacker deploys malware built to destroy data and disable hosts across the control system.
scenarios.source: State-sponsored or politically motivated attacker
scenarios.entryPoint: Any foothold in the control network, often reached through the business network
scenarios.consequence: Loss of the HMIs and servers for days; manual operation or shutdown
vulnerabilities: One domain or shared accounts across hosts
No offline recovery media
No detection of unusual activity

countermeasures.description: Offline backups and a recovery that has been practised
Application allow-listing on critical hosts
Continuous monitoring, with a plan to respond

scenarios.title: Field devices reconfigured
scenarios.statement: Field instruments, drives or remote I/O are reconfigured over a field network or with a handheld configurator, changing their ranges or behaviour.
scenarios.source: Attacker with field network access, or careless maintenance
scenarios.entryPoint: Field network, handheld configurator or instrument management software
scenarios.consequence: Wrong readings or actions at the plant, hidden from the control room
vulnerabilities: Field devices accept changes without authentication
Instrument management software open to many users
No record of field device settings

countermeasures.description: Use device write protection where available
Restrict and log access to instrument management software
Keep a record of field device settings and compare against it

scenarios.title: Control hosts used for web and email
scenarios.statement: An operator or engineer uses a control system host to browse the web or read email, and brings in malware.
scenarios.source: Malware author, helped by staff using control hosts for web and email
scenarios.entryPoint: Web browser or email client on a control system host
scenarios.consequence: Malware inside the control zone
vulnerabilities: Internet access allowed from the control zone
General-purpose software installed on control hosts
Users with administrator rights

countermeasures.description: Block internet and email access from the control zone
Remove software not needed for operation
Do day-to-day work without administrator rights

scenarios.title: Single point of failure brings a long outage
scenarios.statement: An attacker disables a single critical server or switch, by a crafted message or by deleting its configuration, and with no redundancy or tested recovery the control system stays down.
scenarios.source: Attacker with network access
scenarios.entryPoint: Single points of failure in the control system
scenarios.consequence: Extended loss of view or control; process shutdown
vulnerabilities: No redundancy for critical servers or network paths
Uninterruptible power supplies not maintained
Recovery depends on one person's knowledge

countermeasures.description: Redundancy for critical functions, with a tested failover
Emergency power sized and maintained for the control system
Written recovery procedures

scenarios.title: False time, name or address services
scenarios.statement: An attacker or a misconfiguration supplies false time, name or address information to control system hosts, so records and sessions become unreliable.
scenarios.source: Attacker with network access, or a misconfiguration
scenarios.entryPoint: Time, name and address services on the control network
scenarios.consequence: Unreliable logs, failed authentication, devices pointed at the wrong server
vulnerabilities: Time and address services accept answers from any host
The control zone relies on business network services
No alert when the time jumps

countermeasures.description: Provide protected time and network services inside the control zone
Alert on time changes and address conflicts
Limit which hosts may provide these services

scenarios.title: Integrator leaves hidden access behind
scenarios.statement: An integrator leaves an undocumented account, remote support tool or modem in place after a project, and it is later found and used.
scenarios.source: Former contractor, or an attacker who finds the access
scenarios.entryPoint: Undocumented accounts, remote desktop tools or modems
scenarios.consequence: An unmonitored route into the control system
vulnerabilities: No check of accounts and connections at handover
Remote support tools installed without approval
Accounts with no named owner

countermeasures.description: Check accounts, tools and connections at project handover
Approve and list every remote support tool
Review accounts regularly and disable those not used

scenarios.title: Change to shared network equipment cuts control traffic
scenarios.statement: A change made by IT staff to core switches shared with the business network, such as a firmware update or VLAN change, delays or cuts control and safety traffic.
scenarios.source: IT staff or an IT service provider
scenarios.entryPoint: Shared switches, VLANs or links
scenarios.consequence: Delayed or lost control messages; safety trips
vulnerabilities: VLANs used as the only separation
Core switches shared with business systems
No limits on traffic between VLANs

countermeasures.description: Separate control and safety networks from business traffic
Filter traffic at zone boundaries
Protect control traffic from overload

scenarios.title: Telemetry link to a remote site misused
scenarios.statement: An attacker with access to the cellular, radio or leased line link to a remote site sends false commands to its RTU, or alters the readings it reports to the control centre.
scenarios.source: Attacker with access to the telemetry network or to a remote site
scenarios.entryPoint: Telemetry link between the control centre and the remote RTUs
scenarios.consequence: Remote plant operated without the control room knowing, or false readings acted on
vulnerabilities: Telemetry protocols that do not check who sent a message
Cellular modems with public addresses or factory settings
Remote sites unmanned and rarely visited

countermeasures.description: Authenticate the RTUs and the control centre to each other
Protect telemetry messages against alteration where the protocol and the devices allow
Accept telemetry only from known sites at the control centre boundary, and route engineering access to the sites through the managed remote access service

scenarios.title: IT management tool used against control hosts
scenarios.statement: An attacker who takes over a directory service or IT management tool shared with the business network uses it to push malicious software or settings to every control host at once.
scenarios.source: Attacker who has taken over the business network's administration
scenarios.entryPoint: Shared directory service, software deployment or remote management tool
scenarios.consequence: Every managed control host compromised or disabled at the same time
vulnerabilities: Control hosts joined to the business directory
IT administrator accounts with rights on control hosts
Deployment tools that can reach the control zone

countermeasures.description: Manage control hosts from a directory and tools inside the control system, not from the business network
Keep administrator accounts for control hosts separate, limited to the task and reviewed
Allow only approved software to run on control hosts

scenarios.title: Package unit connected without review
scenarios.statement: A supplier's package unit arrives with its own network and remote access, and is connected to the control network without review, opening a path around the zone boundaries.
scenarios.source: Attacker using the package supplier's remote access, or malware already on the unit
scenarios.entryPoint: The package unit's network, or its supplier's remote access or modem
scenarios.consequence: An unmanaged route into the control network, and changes to the unit's control the site does not know about
vulnerabilities: Package units connected by the supplier during commissioning
Supplier modems or remote tools missing from the site's inventory
Package networks bridged into the plant network

countermeasures.description: Treat each package unit as a zone of its own, connected through a reviewed conduit
Bring the supplier's remote access onto the site's managed remote access service
Record the package unit's devices and connections in the site inventory at handover
